lessons.title: Wants, needs and choice

objectives: Tell the difference between wants and needs and between goods and services.

blocks.title: What economics studies
blocks.md: **Economics** studies how people, families, firms and governments use **limited** resources to satisfy **unlimited** wants. **Needs** are things we must have to live (food, water, shelter, clothing). **Wants** are things we would like to have (a phone, a football, fashionable shoes). **Goods** are things you can touch (rice, a book). **Services** are activities done for you (teaching, a haircut, a taxi ride).

blocks.title: Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost
blocks.md: Because resources and money are limited, we cannot satisfy all our wants. This is **scarcity**. We must **choose**. When we choose one thing, we give up another. The **opportunity cost** of a choice is the **next best thing** we give up. A **scale of preference** is a list of wants arranged from the most to the least important.

items.text: A scale of preference (most important first)

blocks.caption: A scale of preference: wants listed from the most to the least important.
blocks.alt: Four stacked boxes numbered one to four showing school fees, food, a football and a cinema ticket.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md: A need for one person may be a want for another: a bicycle is a want for a child but a need for a farmer who must travel far. Opportunity cost is the **one** best alternative given up, not all the things you gave up and not the price you paid. Scarcity does not only affect poor people; everyone must choose.

blocks.title: Free goods and economic goods
blocks.md: A **free good** (such as air in an open place) costs nothing to use and is not scarce. An **economic good** is scarce and has a price (cassava, a mobile phone, a school uniform). Most goods and services are economic goods, so people need money, time and effort to get them.

blocks.title: Worked example — choosing with money
blocks.statement: Etienne has 10 000 FCFA. His list is: school exercise books (4 500 FCFA), a football (3 000 FCFA) and a cinema ticket (4 000 FCFA). He buys the exercise books and the football. How much money is left and what did he give up?
steps: Money left = 10 000 − 7 500 = 2500 FCFA, which is not enough for the cinema ticket (4 000).
He gave up the cinema ticket: that is the opportunity cost of buying both things.
blocks.answer: 2 500 FCFA left; the cinema ticket was given up

blocks.title: Worked example — goods or services
blocks.statement: Sort these into goods and services: a bag of rice, a haircut, a mobile phone, a bus ride.
steps: A bag of rice and a mobile phone are things you can touch: goods.
A haircut and a bus ride are activities done for you.
blocks.answer: Goods: rice, phone. Services: haircut, bus ride

objectives: Name the four factors of production.
Give examples of each and its reward.
Calculate a simple profit from farm accounts.

blocks.title: Factors of production
blocks.md: **Production** is making goods and services. To produce, we need four **factors of production**. **Land** means all natural resources: soil, forests, rivers, minerals. **Labour** is the work of people. **Capital** is man-made equipment used to produce, such as tools, machines and buildings. **Enterprise** is the person who organises the other factors and takes risks: the **entrepreneur**.

blocks.title: Rewards
blocks.md: Each factor earns a reward: land earns **rent**, labour earns **wages**, capital earns **interest** and enterprise earns **profit**. **Profit** is what is left from sales after all costs have been paid. If costs are bigger than sales, there is a **loss**.

blocks.caption: The four factors of production: land, labour, capital and enterprise.
blocks.alt: Four boxes in a row naming the factors.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md: Capital is **not** simply money in the pocket: in economics it is the tools and machines used to make other goods. Do not mix up **rent** (reward for land) with house rent paid by a tenant, although the idea is similar. A worker's tools belong to capital, but the worker is labour. One person can supply more than one factor.

blocks.title: Example from a farm
blocks.md: On a farm in Bali, the field is land, the people who plant and harvest are labour, the hoes and the storage shed are capital and the farmer who plans the planting, buys seed and takes the risk of bad weather is the entrepreneur.

blocks.title: Worked example — farm profit
blocks.statement: Mama Ngu sells crops worth 300 000 FCFA. She pays workers 90 000 FCFA, land rent 40 000 FCFA and 50 000 FCFA for seeds (illustrative). Find her profit.

blocks.title: Worked example — name the factor
blocks.statement: A baker in Limbe uses an oven, hires two helpers, rents the shop and plans the day's baking. Name each factor.
steps: The oven is capital and the shop's land and building are land and capital.
